kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.canonical_name: L293D quadruple half-H bridge motor driver
identity.manufacturer: Texas Instruments (originally a Unitrode design, also second-sourced by STMicroelectronics)
identity.package: PDIP-16 (through-hole, 16-pin dual in-line, with 4 internally tied ground/heat-sink pins)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A chip that lets a small microcontroller pin safely control a motor that needs more current than the microcontroller can supply, and lets you reverse the motor's direction with software instead of by hand.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Spinning one or two small DC motors (or one stepper motor) forward, backward, or at variable speed using PWM, controlled from UNO digital and PWM pins.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Each of its two independent H-bridges acts like 4 switches arranged around the motor; turning on one diagonal pair of switches drives current one way through the motor, turning on the other diagonal pair reverses it. Built-in diodes absorb the voltage spike that happens whenever a motor is switched off.

pinout.name: 1,2EN
pinout.notes: must be HIGH for outputs 1Y/2Y to respond to inputs; can be PWM'd for speed control

pinout.name: GROUND
pinout.notes: connect to common ground and, where possible, a PCB ground plane

pinout.name: GROUND
pinout.notes: connect to common ground and, where possible, a PCB ground plane

pinout.name: 2Y
pinout.notes: connects to the other terminal of the same motor as 1Y

pinout.name: VCC2
pinout.notes: 4.5V to 36V; powers the motor itself, separate from the logic power

pinout.name: 3,4EN
pinout.notes: must be HIGH for outputs 3Y/4Y to respond to inputs; can be PWM'd for speed control

pinout.name: 3Y
pinout.notes: connects to one terminal of a second motor

pinout.name: GROUND
pinout.notes: connect to common ground and, where possible, a PCB ground plane

pinout.name: GROUND
pinout.notes: connect to common ground and, where possible, a PCB ground plane

pinout.name: 4Y
pinout.notes: connects to the other terminal of the second motor

pinout.name: VCC1
pinout.notes: 5V; powers the chip's internal logic and must always be supplied even when VCC2 is a separate battery

pins.pin_1_identification: With the small notch at the top of the chip, pin 1 (1,2EN) is the top-left pin; pin numbers then run counter-clockwise around the package.

electrical.operating_voltage: VCC1 (logic) 4.5V to 7V, typically 5V; VCC2 (motor) can equal VCC1 or run as high as 36V
electrical.typical_current: logic supply current (ICC1) typically 13-35 mA depending on output states (max 22-60 mA); logic input current is only a few to about 100 microamps per input (IIH/IIL)
electrical.max_current: 600 mA continuous output current per channel; 1.2 A peak, non-repetitive, up to 100 microseconds per channel
electrical.logic_level: 5V TTL-compatible inputs (VIH min about 2.3V, VIL max about 1.5V)

key_specs.channels: 4 half-H drivers, usable as 2 independent full H-bridges
key_specs.built_in_flyback_diodes: yes, only on the L293D variant; the plain L293 needs external diodes

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Black rectangular plastic chip with 16 pins in two rows of 8, a standard 0.3-inch-wide DIP package about 20mm long.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Black plastic body printed with 'L293D' plus a manufacturer logo and date code (e.g. L293DNE); a small notch or dimple marks the pin-1 end.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: L293D (sometimes with a manufacturer prefix/suffix such as L293DNE)
easily_confused_with: 74HC595 (identical 16-pin DIP body size and colour, distinguishable only by the printed part number)
ULN2003 driver chip (a different pinout but a similarly sized black DIP body)

example_connections.uno_pin: 5V (tied high), or a PWM pin (e.g. Digital 5) for speed control
Digital pin (direction control, opposite state of 1A)
Power Supply Module output (per ELEGOO's Lesson 21), or the UNO's own 5V for light testing only

required_extra_parts: Fan blade and 3-6V motor (or another small DC motor)
Power Supply Module plus a 9V adapter (recommended over powering the motor from the UNO)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required; driven with plain digitalWrite()/analogWrite()

hazards: The chip can get noticeably warm driving a motor near its current limit; thermal shutdown protects it but repeated overheating shortens its life
Never connect a motor directly to an UNO pin; always go through this chip or a similar driver
handling_notes: Always connect VCC1 (logic) even when VCC2 (motor power) comes from a separate battery, or the chip will not respond to inputs
Tie unused enable pins HIGH, not left floating
Keep the four ground pins, which double as the heat sink, well connected to a solid ground for better heat dissipation
common_mistakes: Forgetting to power VCC1 separately from VCC2 and assuming one supply covers both
Leaving an enable pin floating or LOW and wondering why the motor will not move
Exceeding 600 mA continuous per channel with a bigger motor than the kit's small fan motor

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Motor does not move at all
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: The enable pin (1,2EN or 3,4EN) is LOW or unconnected, or VCC1 is not powered
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure DC voltage at pin 1 (or pin 9) and at pin 16 with a multimeter; both should read close to 5V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Motor spins one direction only and ignores commands to reverse
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: One of the two input pins (1A/2A) is stuck HIGH or LOW, often from a bad jumper
symptoms_and_causes.check: Probe 1A and 2A while the sketch toggles them, confirming both actually change state

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: The motor is drawing close to or beyond 600 mA per channel
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure current in series with the motor supply line; if it is consistently near or above 600 mA, use a lower-current motor or a driver rated for more current

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the board powered and a test sketch running, use DC voltage mode to check VCC1 (pin 16) to GND reads about 5V, and VCC2 (pin 8) to GND reads the motor supply voltage. Then probe an output pin (e.g. 1Y) to GND while toggling its matching input; it should swing between about 0V and close to VCC2 as the input changes.
